title: Activation Clustering False Assurance: Benign and Harmful Prompts Share Residual Stream Neighborhoods

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tests whether activation clustering provides a useful safety signal. If harmful and benign prompts are inseparable, clustering-based monitoring is ineffective. Useful finding but somewhat expected given known embedding space properties.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Collecting activations, running UMAP, and k-means clustering are standard data science tasks well within beginner CS student capability. No SAE training required, just forward passes and standard ML tools. Medium compute easily sufficient.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Very tight deliverable: UMAP visualizations and separability metrics (silhouette score, etc.) at each layer for harmful vs. benign prompts. Single clean experiment with clear output. 30 hours is ample.

novelty.reasoning: This is substantially addressed by existing work that directly contradicts the premise. (1) 'Defending Large Language Models Against Attacks With Residual Stream Activation Analysis' (arXiv:2406.03230, 2024) trains LightGBM classifiers on residual activations and finds 'significant separation between classes in the residual activation representational space' with consistently high accuracy and low false negative rates across all layers — directly showing harmful and benign prompts ARE separable. (2) 'N-GLARE' (arXiv:2511.14195, 2025) uses latent representations for LLM safety evaluation. (3) Research on Jensen-Shannon Separability shows safety-aligned LLMs exhibit well-separated activation trajectories. The hypothesis that clustering fails is contradicted by existing evidence showing it works well, at least for standard attack types. The idea may still have value for adversarial/stealthy prompts, but the baseline claim is already addressed.
